title: Exact and inexact subsampled Newton methods for optimization
contribution: Sampling rules for subsampled Newton methods (geometric gradient growth with constant Hessian sample gives R-linear, faster-than-geometric gradient growth with any growing Hessian sample gives R-superlinear convergence in expectation) and a work-complexity analysis of inexact subsampled Newton-CG compared with Newton-SGI/LiSSA and Newton sketch; read as arXiv v1 (pp. 6, 11, 16, 18-21).
problem_entry: Which gradient/Hessian sample sequences {X_k},{S_k} are most promising in theory and practice (p. 2), and whether CG, the accepted inner solver in deterministic Newton, stays preferable to a stochastic gradient iteration under subsampling, measured by the effort to reach a local linear rate 1/2 (p. 3).
key_idea: Coordinate sample sizes with the target rate (Thm 2.1 p. 6; Thm 2.4 pp. 8, 11); in the inexact method fix beta and the CG count r (or residual forcing zeta <= mu_beta/(8L)) so each error term is at most 1/8 of the contraction (pp. 16-17).
assumptions: Each F_i strongly convex (via regularization), bounded subsampled-Hessian eigenvalues, bounded gradient covariance trace, Lipschitz Hessian, bounded Hessian-component variance (A1-A4, pp. 5-6); restrictive moment assumption B1 (pp. 11, 27); independent uniform samples (pp. 6, 27).
proof_devices: three-term split of the expected Newton-step error: Lipschitz-Hessian, Hessian-subsampling and gradient-sampling terms (Lemma 2.2, pp. 8-9)
variance of a sample mean via the trace of a covariance, with Jensen (eq. 2.11, p. 7; Lemma 2.3, p. 10)
Hessian error measured along w_k - w* instead of matrix concentration inequalities (p. 10), removing a log d factor in the complexity comparison (p. 19)
induction on E||w_k - w*|| with fixed error shares 1/4, 1/8, 1/8 (Theorem 3.2, p. 16)
worst-case CG bound in sqrt(kappa) plugged into a linear-quadratic recursion (eq. 3.4, p. 14; Lemma 3.1, p. 14)
work counted in Hessian-vector products to reach a rate of 1/2: Newton-CG O(kmax^2 min{d, sqrt(kmax) log kmax}) vs LiSSA O(kmax^2 k log k log d) (eqs. 4.1, 4.4, pp. 18-19)
experiments: L2-regularized logistic regression on six binary datasets (Table 5.1, p. 22): GD, Newton, Newton-CG at |S| = 5/10/50%, Newton-SGI; error vs iterations, effective gradient evaluations and CPU time (pp. 23-24); CG parameters fixed in advance and untuned (p. 22), SGI given matched Hessian-vector budget and a step-length grid (pp. 24, 26); CG and SGI similar in evaluations, SGI slower in time (p. 24).
positioning: N.B. paragraph distinguishing results in expectation for the whole sequence from Xu et al.'s one-step results in probability (p. 3); same contrast with Roosta-Khorasani and Mahoney and with Pasupathy et al. (pp. 4, 13); Table 4.1 presented as a literature summary, not a ranking (pp. 20-21).
writing: Hedged verdicts: no result in the area is called definitive (p. 13); numerical results labelled preliminary (pp. 1, 27); caveats on worst-case CG (p. 17) and on mixed convergence types in Table 4.1 (p. 21).
limits_future: Limits: assumption B1, uniform sampling only, worst-case CG analysis, theory demanding kappa^2 samples while practice needs few, preliminary numerics (pp. 11, 17, 20, 27); future: comprehensive numerical study and proof techniques beyond concentration bounds (pp. 20, 27).

method_links.note: Own CG parameters (zeta = 0.01, maxcg = 10) fixed beforehand and untuned; the rival SGI gets a matched Hessian-vector budget and a step-length grid 2^-20..2^3.

Theory separates the inner solvers (sqrt(kappa) vs kappa, log d), but runs show them similar in effective gradient evaluations, no bound-vs-run plot is given, the sample-size theory is admitted to be pessimistic, and Table 4.1 is said not to rank methods.

The received view that CG is the inner solver of choice is retested under subsampling; here the classical tool is defended against a newer challenger (LiSSA-type SGI), with a scoped verdict that both deserve more study.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Constant Hessian sample suffices for R-linear and any growth to infinity for R-superlinear convergence, while the gradient sample must grow geometrically or faster.
Hessian sample size and CG iterations (or residual forcing zeta <= mu_beta/(8L)) chosen so the sampling and CG-residual error terms are each at most 1/8 of the contraction.

transferable: Compare two inner solvers by the work, in one shared unit (Hessian-vector products), each needs to reach a common target such as a local linear rate with constant 1/2 (pp. 3, 18).
Bound a subsampled-matrix error along the single relevant vector (w_k - w*) via the trace of a covariance instead of a matrix concentration inequality; it removes a log d factor (pp. 10, 19).
Prove a target contraction by giving each error term a fixed share (1/4 quadratic, 1/8 sampling, 1/8 solver) and solving for the sample size and iteration count each share implies (p. 16).
When a concurrent paper posts similar-looking results, add a dated paragraph stating the difference in result type (in expectation for the sequence vs one step in probability) and scope (pp. 3, 13).
In a work-complexity table, state per row the convergence type and accuracy measure and say that the table does not rank methods (pp. 20-21).
coauthors: Raghu Bollapragada (Northwestern IEMS), Richard Byrd (University of Colorado, Computer Science)

quotes.text: all the results just mentioned are useful and shed light into the properties of subsampled Newton methods, but none of them seem to be definitive.
This suggests that the theory could be improved and that techniques other than concentration bounds might help in achieving this.

title: Adaptive finite-difference interval estimation for noisy derivative-free optimization
contribution: A bisection procedure that, given the noise level, finds a near-optimal finite-difference interval for any difference scheme by driving a computable truncation-to-measurement error ratio into a band, without estimating higher derivatives, with a finite-termination theorem and tests in 1-D and in FD L-BFGS on 54 noisy CUTEst problems; read as arXiv v2 (pp. 1, 4-5, 8, 12, 15-19).
problem_entry: Noise has kept finite differences out of favour in DFO because the interval becomes critical as noise grows (p. 1); the near-optimal interval needs a higher derivative that users do not have (p. 2), and the default sqrt(eps_M) rule fails under noise (p. 2).
key_idea: Estimate h directly: bisect h until a testing ratio, e.g. |f(t+4h) - 4f(t+h) + 3f(t)|/(8 eps_f), lies in [r_l, r_u] with r_l > 1, r_u > r_l + 2, giving h of optimal order; generalized to any scheme with testing ratios built from the scheme at h and alpha*h, reusing evaluations (pp. 4-5, 8, 10-11).
assumptions: Bounded noise |eps(t)| <= eps_f with eps_f known (Assumption 3.1, pp. 12, 15, 19); ratio-perturbation bound from ||w~||_1 = 1 and continuity with r_S(2^K h_0) >= r_u - 1 (Assumptions 3.2-3.3, p. 12); o(h^q) ignored in the accuracy argument (pp. 4, 9); uniform noise in tests (p. 14).
proof_devices: Taylor argument bounding the noise part of the testing ratio by 1 so that h lands within a constant factor of h* (eqs. 2.6-2.8, pp. 4-5; eqs. 3.7-3.10, pp. 8-9)

finite termination by contradiction: invariants r_S(l_k) < r_l + 1 and r_S(u_k) > r_u - 1 on the true function, finite expansion phase, uniform continuity on a compact bracket (Theorem 3.4, pp. 12-13)
as printed, Theorem 3.4 states 0 < r_l while Algorithm 3.1 requires 1 < r_l, and the proof uses expansion factor 2 while the algorithm has a general eta (pp. 8, 12-13)
failure-case analysis in prose: o(h^q) dominance, phi^(q) ~ 0 ending in a warning after max iter 20, termination at risk if eps_f is underestimated (pp. 11-12)
experiments: 1-D: six schemes (Table 1, p. 14) on cos(t) for eps_f from 1e-8 to 1e-1 and four difficult functions, with h-dagger marked on the worst-case relative-error curve (Figs. 1-2, pp. 15-16); FD L-BFGS (memory 10, relaxed Armijo-Wolfe) on 54 CUTEst problems at eps_f in {1e-1, 1e-3, 1e-5, 1e-7}, Fixed (idealized, true Hessian info) vs More-Wild vs Adaptive, optimality gap vs function evaluations (Table 2, Figs. 3-4, pp. 16-19), full tables in App. B (pp. 32-39).
positioning: Places itself in numerical differentiation (Curtis-Reid, Stepleman-Winarsky, Gill-Murray-Saunders-Wright, Barton, More-Wild; p. 3); contrasts with Gill et al.'s nested estimation and More-Wild's non-affine-invariant test (p. 6); Gill et al. dropped from the benchmark since More-Wild is regarded as an improvement (p. 17).
writing: Practical considerations numbered I-V (rule choice, ratio generation, initialization, special cases, sensitivity to eps_f), pairing each failure case with its design rule (pp. 10-12).
limits_future: Limits: known noise level, rare large errors from poor h_0 (BOX2), higher cost than More-Wild and than the idealized Fixed interval, termination needs eps_f not underestimated (pp. 11-12, 19, 31); future: unbounded finite-variance noise via Chebyshev and periodic re-estimation of the interval (p. 19).

method_links.note: FD L-BFGS engine kept; only the difference interval is replaced, driven by eps_f; the unknowable higher derivative is replaced by a testable ratio; misestimated eps_f analysed; phi^(q) ~ 0 ends in a warning, not a failure.
Idealized Fixed baseline using true Hessian information, not viable in practice; rival More-Wild given a safeguard threshold tuned on the test set; own higher cost and the BOX2 failure printed.

Programme context: opens with the DFO community's dismissal of finite differences under noise and closes that accuracy and robustness make them reliable for established algorithms; the broad test is in S080.
Only finite termination is proved; accuracy rests on a Taylor argument checked by plotting the error model with the output marked; the superiority over More-Wild is purely empirical.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Computable proxy for an unavailable quantity
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The testing ratio stands in for the unknown truncation-to-measurement error ratio and hence for |phi^(q)(t)|, and drives the interval search.
Fixed interval computed from true Hessian diagonals (forward differences) or true-Hessian third-derivative estimates (central differences), labelled for benchmarking purposes only.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: invariance as a design requirement and a test
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Testing ratio built to be affine-invariant, rival More-Wild condition (2.12) criticised for not being so, invariance tested on a*sin(b*t).

transferable: To set a parameter that balances two error sources, compute a ratio of the two from available data and bisect the parameter until the ratio lies in a band wider than the ratio's noise bound (r_u > r_l + 2 when the noise part is at most 1), instead of estimating the constant in the optimal formula (pp. 4-5, 8-9).

Generate valid testing ratios for any difference scheme by combining the scheme at h and alpha*h, which cancels the derivative term and reuses evaluations; choose alpha as a power of the expansion factor so monotone trials cost one new evaluation (pp. 5, 10-11).

Evaluate an estimator on a deterministic worst-case error curve against the parameter, with the estimator's output marked, so the check needs no noise realization (eq. 4.1, p. 14; Figs. 1-2, pp. 15-16).
Add an oracle arm with true derivative information, labelled for benchmarking only, to show the distance between a practical rule and the ideal (pp. 17-18).
For each user-supplied estimate, write the direction of failure when it is wrong: overestimated eps_f still terminates with h > h*, underestimated eps_f may not terminate and gives h < h* (p. 12).
coauthors: Hao-Jun Michael Shi, Yuchen Xie, Melody Qiming Xuan (all Northwestern IEMS)

quotes.text: Our procedure produces reliable estimates of the finite-difference interval at low cost without explicitly approximating higher-order derivatives.
We created this idealized option for benchmarking purposes only.
